'''''Senna septemtrionalis''''', commonly known as '''arsenic bush''',<ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Randell |first1=Barbara R. |last2=Barlow |first2=Bryan A. |title=''Senna septemtrionalis'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Senna~septemtrionalis |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is native to Central America, the southern United States and Mexico, but is naturalised in many other countries. It is an erect shrub with [[Pinnation|pinnate]] leaves, with four or five pairs of egg-shaped leaflets, and yellow flowers arranged in groups of five to eight, usually with seven fertile [[stamen]]s and four [[staminode]]s in each flower.

==Description==
''Senna septemtrionalis'' is an erect, [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]] shrub that typically grows to a height of up to {{cvt|3|m}}. Its leaves are pinnate, {{cvt|60–80|mm}} long including a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|15–30|mm}} long, with four or five pairs of egg-shaped leaflets. The leaflets are {{cvt|45–70|mm}} long and {{cvt|15–28|mm}} wide, usually spaced {{cvt|15–30|mm}} apart. There are three or four erect, club-shaped [[Gland (botany)|gland]]s between the lowest pairs of leaflets. The flowers are yellow and arranged on the ends of branches and in upper leaf axils in groups of five to eight on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|30–40|mm}} long, each flower on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] {{cvt|10–13|mm}} long. The petals are up to {{cvt|8|mm}} long and there are usually seven fertile stamens, the [[Stamen#anther|anthers]] {{cvt|4–6|mm}} long and of different lengths, as well as four staminodes. Flowering occurs from April to September in the Southern Hemisphere, and the fruit is a cylindrical [[Glossary of plant morphology#Fruit types|pod]] {{cvt|50–80|mm}} long and {{cvt|10–15|mm}} wide.<ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Senna septemtrionalis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Senna%20septemtrionalis |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
This species was first formally described in 1802 by [[Domenico Viviani]] who gave it the name ''Cassia septemtrionalis'' in ''Elenchus Plantarum Horti Botanici J. Car. Dinegro Observationibus quod Novas, vel Rariores Species Passim Interjectis.''<ref name="APNI1">{{cite web |title=''Cassia septemtrionalis'' |url=https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/592868|publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="Viviani">{{cite book |last1=Viviani |first1=Domenico |title=Elenchus Plantarum Horti Botanici J. Car. Dinegro |date=1802 |publisher=Typis De Planis |location=Genoa |page=14 |url=https://archive.org/details/viviani-dinegro-1802/page/n13/mode/2up |access-date=9 December 2024}}</ref> In 1982, [[Howard Samuel Irwin]] and [[Rupert Charles Barneby]] transferred the species to the genus ''[[Senna (plant)|Senna]]'' as ''S. septemtrionalis'' in the ''[[Memoirs of the New York Botanical Garden]]''.<ref name="APNI">{{cite web |title=''Senna septemtrionalis'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/602656 |publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=28 August 2023}}</ref> The [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''septemtrionalis'') means "north" or "northern".<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |author=[[William T. Stearn]] |title=Botanical Latin. History, grammar, syntax, terminology and vocabulary |date=1992 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Oregon |edition=4th|page=492}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Senna septemtrionalis'' is native to the southern United States, Mexico and central America, but is introduced to many other countries, including to Queensland and New South Wales in Australia, and its offshore islands, [[Lord Howe Island|Lord Howe]] and [[Norfolk Island]]s. In Australia it is found in pastures and disturbed rainforest.<ref name="POWO" /><ref name="RBGS" /><ref name="foa" />
